Set ventricular sensitivity to its least sensitive value before surgery
Insert a precautionary temporary transvenous pacing wire
Program an asynchronous DOO mode for the whole procedure
commentaires: Correct: the surgical field and current path are far from the can; general precautions suffice in this pacing-dependent patient.
Incorrect: very low sensitivity risks undersensing and would not reliably protect against nearby interference.
Incorrect: invasive temporary pacing has no indication when the pacemaker is working normally.
Incorrect: below the umbilicus the risk of interference is very low; routine asynchronous pacing is unnecessary and competes with sinus rhythm.

The risk of inhibition by monopolar diathermy depends on the distance between the surgical field and the can and on the current path between the diathermy tip and the return pad. For hip surgery with the pad on the thigh, the current flows far from the chest: the HRS/ASA and EHRA consensus documents do not require reprogramming. General precautions apply: short bursts, bipolar diathermy when possible, continuous ECG and pulse oximetry monitoring, a magnet and a means of external pacing at hand. Good habit: reason on the patient's dependency and on the location of the surgical field, not merely on the presence of a pacemaker.

In a pacing-dependent patient operated on above the umbilicus, an asynchronous mode (VOO/DOO) is programmed or a magnet is applied, which makes a pacemaker pace asynchronously at a manufacturer-specific rate. In all cases: return pad positioned so that the current path runs away from the can, short bursts (< 5 s), bipolar diathermy when possible, ECG and pulse oximetry monitoring, external pacing available. A device check is recommended after the procedure if the device was reprogrammed or if significant interference occurred.

Upgrade to CRT or to conduction system pacing
Lengthen the AV delay to 300 ms to allow intrinsic conduction
Enable a ventricular pacing reduction algorithm

Risk factors are a high RV pacing burden, a wide paced QRS and a low LVEF before implantation. Asynchronous DOO mode, slightly faster than the intrinsic rhythm
Non-pacing ODO mode, since sinus rhythm is present

Good habit: decide the MRI mode from the patient's dependency, then restore the initial settings after the scan.

ECG and oximetry monitoring during the scan, with someone able to reprogram the device. Non-MR-conditional systems can also be scanned within a structured protocol (class IIa). Device check and restoration of the initial programming at the end of the scan.

cas-egmp-004.question: Emergency department: a 71-year-old woman with a DDD pacemaker for complete AV block (maximum tracking rate 130 bpm) is admitted with acute dyspnoea; SpO2 89%, raised D-dimer. Pacemaker-mediated tachycardia: apply the magnet to terminate it
Tracking of atrial flutter: mode switching must be enabled urgently
Normal sinus tachycardia tracking: find its cause (embolism?)
commentaires: Incorrect: sensor-driven pacing would begin with an AP, not with a sensed P wave.
Incorrect: there are no retrograde P waves at a fixed VA interval and the rate remains below the maximum tracking rate.

Good habit: a patient with complete AV block paced in DDD has the ventricular rate of his atrium; a paced sinus tachycardia is treated by treating its cause.
cas-egmp-004.aRetenir: Paced tachycardia in DDD: if every VP follows a sensed sinus P wave, this is normal tracking; treat the cause of the sinus tachycardia.
cas-egmp-004.rappel: In DDD mode, any P wave sensed outside the refractory period starts an AV delay followed by a VP, up to the maximum tracking rate. The markers and the atrial EGM settle the question. A magnet makes the pacemaker asynchronous: it terminates pacemaker-mediated tachycardia but has no role in an appropriate sinus tachycardia.

cas-egmp-005.question: An 86-year-old woman had a DDD pacemaker implanted 11 years ago for syncope with documented second-degree Mobitz II AV block; the device has reached the elective replacement indicator (ERI). False

Good habit: a low pacing percentage is no proof that a paroxysmal block has resolved.

cas-egmp-005.rappel: ESC 2021: second-degree Mobitz II, high-grade and complete AV block are indications for pacing (class I) irrespective of symptoms, in the absence of a reversible cause. ERI usually leaves about 3 months before the device reaches end of service, depending on the manufacturer.

Program AAIR mode, since conduction is masked by the AV delay
Lower the base rate to 45 bpm to give way to sinus rhythm
Return to a physiological AV delay and accept pacing

cas-egmp-010.question: Day hospital: a 70-year-old man with a DDD pacemaker (right pectoral can) for paroxysmal AV block, and symptomatic persistent AF on well-managed anticoagulation for 5 weeks. cas-egmp-010.aRetenir: Cardioversion in a pacemaker recipient: antero-posterior pads away from the can, then a device check.

The current can transiently raise the threshold at the electrode-tissue interface. A magnet does not protect the circuit: it only makes pacing asynchronous. Mode switching during AF is the expected behaviour: switch to a non-tracking mode (DDI or VDI depending on the manufacturer).

cas-egmp-011.question: Device clinic: a resident shows you this stored episode from a patient with a DDD pacemaker and is surprised by the many AR markers within the rapid atrial activity. False

An AR event is seen by the device: it does not start an AV delay, which prevents tracking of the arrhythmia, but it is counted to estimate the atrial rate. This counting led to the MS marker, followed by irregular VS in a non-tracking mode. Conversely, a signal falling in a blanking period is neither sensed nor marked, which can lead to underestimation of the atrial rate. Post-ventricular atrial blanking (PVAB) protects against far-field ventricular sensing but can hide every other flutter wave in 2:1 flutter. Mode switching relies on the measured atrial rate, with manufacturer-specific rate and duration criteria, and switches to a non-tracking mode (DDI(R) or VDI(R)).

cas-egmp-013.question: Emergency department: a 67-year-old man with a DDD pacemaker for AV block (maximum tracking rate 130 bpm) has had palpitations since the previous day, with a regular paced tachycardia at 125 bpm and blood pressure 115/70 mmHg. The fall in rate with the magnet ruled out an underlying atrial arrhythmia

Good habit: faced with a paced tachycardia, interrogate the device before drawing conclusions.
